warmup.q: A test starts 2 threads that each call a racy hit() 1,000 times, then checks the total. It passes 20 runs out of 20. What is the most likely reason?
options: The counter is thread-safe after all
The first thread usually finishes before the second one starts, so they never overlap
JUnit runs threads one at a time
warmup.why: 1,000 increments take microseconds, about as long as starting a thread. The first thread is often done before the second begins, so there is no interleaving to go wrong. The test proves nothing. Make the threads start together with a latch, use more of them, and run far more iterations, as this lesson shows.

sections.h: A concurrency test has to make threads collide
sections.html:
A race only shows up when threads overlap at the wrong moment. A test that doesn't force overlap is a single-threaded test with extra steps. Five habits turn it into a stress test:

  • Hold every thread at a start latch and release them together. Lesson 3 of this track built this.
  • Use more threads than cores, so the scheduler interleaves them.
  • Run many operations per thread, so the threads overlap for a long time.
  • Run many rounds with a fresh state each time. One round is one sample of the interleavings.
  • Check an invariant when all threads are done: totals that must add up, an amount that must never be exceeded. Never assert on timings.

The lab packs those habits into a small harness, shaped like jcstress: a setup that builds fresh state, an actor that every thread runs over and over, and an invariant checked after join(). The figure shows one round.

Java
record Round(RefundLedger ledger, AtomicLong approved) {}

int failed = Stress.failingRounds(20, 8, 2_000,
        () -> new Round(new RefundLedger(Map.of("pay-1", 10_000L)), new AtomicLong()),   // fresh state per round
        r -> { if (r.ledger().refund("pay-1", 1)) r.approved().incrementAndGet(); },      // every thread, over and over
        r -> r.approved().get() == 10_000 && r.ledger().refunded("pay-1") == 10_000);     // must hold at the end
assertThat(failed).isZero();
Kotlin
class Round(val ledger: RefundLedger, val approved: AtomicLong)

val failed = Stress.failingRounds(20, 8, 2_000,
    { Round(RefundLedger(mapOf("pay-1" to 10_000L)), AtomicLong()) },              // fresh state per round
    { r -> if (r.ledger.refund("pay-1", 1)) r.approved.incrementAndGet() },        // every thread, over and over
    { r -> r.approved.get() == 10_000L && r.ledger.refunded("pay-1") == 10_000L }) // must hold at the end
assertThat(failed).isZero()

Eight threads try 2,000 one-cent refunds each against 10,000 cents captured, so a correct ledger approves exactly 10,000. The racy ledger in the lab approves all 16,000.

Two more rules keep these tests from hurting you. Put a timeout on every one, with JUnit's @Timeout or assertTimeoutPreemptively, so a deadlock fails the test in seconds instead of hanging CI for an hour. And remember what a pass means: this run found no failure. A stress test can prove that a race exists. It can never prove that one doesn't, which is why the design rules from earlier lessons matter more than any test.

try.title: The same bug, tested two ways
steps: Read NaiveVsStress. It tests the racy counter from lesson 3 twenty times the usual way (2 threads, 1,000 hits, no start line), then twenty times as a stress test (8 threads, 100,000 hits, start latch).
Predict how many runs of each fail.
Run it two or three times.

code.title: NaiveVsStress.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l13; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; /** The same racy counter, tested twice: the way most tests are written, and the way that finds the bug. */ public class NaiveVsStress { static final class Counter { volatile int count; // volatile only stops the JIT from hiding the race (lesson 3) void hit() { count++; } // the bug: read, add, write } // 2 threads, 1,000 hits each, no start line static boolean naiveRound() throws InterruptedException { Counter c = new Counter(); Thread a = new Thread(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) c.hit(); }); Thread b = new Thread(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) c.hit(); }); a.start(); b.start(); a.join(); b.join(); return c.count == 2_000; } // 8 threads, 100,000 hits each, released together static boolean stressRound() throws InterruptedException { Counter c = new Counter(); CountDownLatch go = new CountDownLatch(1); Thread[] ts = new Thread[8]; for (int t = 0; t < ts.length; t++) { ts[t] = new Thread(() -> { try { go.await(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; } for (int i = 0; i < 100_000; i++) c.hit(); }); ts[t].start(); } go.countDown(); for (Thread t : ts) t.join(); return c.count == 800_000; } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { int naiveFailed = 0, stressFailed = 0; for (int r = 0; r < 20; r++) if (!naiveRound()) naiveFailed++; for (int r = 0; r < 20; r++) if (!stressRound()) stressFailed++; System.out.println("naive test (2 threads x 1,000, no start line): failed " + naiveFailed + " of 20 runs"); System.out.println("stress test (8 threads x 100,000, start latch): failed " + stressFailed + " of 20 runs"); } }

alt.title: NaiveVsStress.kt
alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l13 import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch import kotlin.concurrent.thread // The same racy counter, tested twice: the way most tests are written, and the way that finds the bug. private class RacyCounter { @Volatile var count = 0 // @Volatile only stops the JIT from hiding the race (lesson 3) fun hit() { count++ } // the bug: read, add, write } // 2 threads, 1,000 hits each, no start line private fun naiveRound(): Boolean { val c = RacyCounter() val a = thread { repeat(1_000) { c.hit() } } val b = thread { repeat(1_000) { c.hit() } } a.join(); b.join() return c.count == 2_000 } // 8 threads, 100,000 hits each, released together private fun stressRound(): Boolean { val c = RacyCounter() val go = CountDownLatch(1) val ts = List(8) { thread { go.await(); repeat(100_000) { c.hit() } } } go.countDown() ts.forEach { it.join() } return c.count == 800_000 } fun main() { val naiveFailed = (1..20).count { !naiveRound() } val stressFailed = (1..20).count { !stressRound() } println("naive test (2 threads x 1,000, no start line): failed $naiveFailed of 20 runs") println("stress test (8 threads x 100,000, start latch): failed $stressFailed of 20 runs") }

try.expect: The naive test fails rarely, 0 to 6 runs of 20 here, and a different number each time. The stress test fails 20 of 20. Same code, same bug. Only the second test is worth having in CI.

sections.h: Replace sleeps with latches, and guesses with deadlines
sections.html:
Thread.sleep in a test is a guess about how long something takes. On your laptop the guess is generous and the test is slow. On a busy CI machine the guess is too short and the test fails for no reason. Both are bad, and the second teaches the team to ignore red builds.

Wait for the event itself, and use the timeout only as a deadline far above any real duration:

Java
// flaky: hopes 50 ms is enough on every machine, and is slow on all of them
worker.submit(payment);
Thread.sleep(50);
assertThat(store.status(payment.id())).isEqualTo(SETTLED);

// solid: wait for the event itself, with a deadline far above any real duration
CountDownLatch settled = new CountDownLatch(1);
store.onSettled(id -> settled.countDown());
worker.submit(payment);
assertThat(settled.await(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS)).isTrue();
assertThat(store.status(payment.id())).isEqualTo(SETTLED);
Kotlin
// flaky: hopes 50 ms is enough on every machine, and is slow on all of them
worker.submit(payment)
Thread.sleep(50)
assertThat(store.status(payment.id)).isEqualTo(SETTLED)

// solid: wait for the event itself, with a deadline far above any real duration
val settled = CountDownLatch(1)
store.onSettled { settled.countDown() }
worker.submit(payment)
assertThat(settled.await(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS)).isTrue()
assertThat(store.status(payment.id)).isEqualTo(SETTLED)

The latch version is fast when things are fast and patient when the machine is slow. It also gives you a clear failure, "not settled within 10 s", instead of a wrong status.

The same tools let you hold a thread at a known point, which makes many concurrency tests deterministic. Give the code under test a fake dependency that blocks on a latch:

Java
class BlockingIssuer implements Issuer {
    final CountDownLatch inCall = new CountDownLatch(1);
    final CountDownLatch release = new CountDownLatch(1);

    @Override
    public Result authorize(Request r) throws InterruptedException {
        inCall.countDown();          // 1. tell the test: a thread is inside the call
        release.await();             // 2. hold it here until the test says go
        return Result.APPROVED;
    }
}
Kotlin
class BlockingIssuer : Issuer {
    val inCall = CountDownLatch(1)
    val release = CountDownLatch(1)

    override fun authorize(r: Request): Result {
        inCall.countDown()           // 1. tell the test: a thread is inside the call
        release.await()              // 2. hold it here until the test says go
        return Result.APPROVED
    }
}

Now the test can wait on inCall, then check what other threads see while one is known to be inside the call. With the IssuerGate from lesson 10 set to one permit, a second caller with a 100 ms limit must time out. Then the test opens release and checks the clean-up. No sleeps, no luck.

When there's no hook to wait on, poll for the condition with a short sleep and an overall deadline, rather than sleeping once and hoping. Checking Thread.getState() until the threads you expect are BLOCKED or WAITING is a common way to know they have queued up. The worked example uses it.

try.title: Make a test flaky on purpose
steps: Read SleepVsLatch. Eight threads burn every core, like a busy CI box. A background worker settles a payment in about 2 ms.
One test sleeps 3 ms and checks; the other waits on a latch for up to 5 seconds. Each runs 100 times. Predict the failure counts.
Run it, then change the sleep to 10 ms and run it again.

code.title: SleepVsLatch.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l13; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; /** * A test checks that a background worker settles a payment. One version sleeps 3 ms and hopes; * the other waits on a latch. Both run 100 times while 8 threads keep every core busy, like a CI box. */ public class SleepVsLatch { static volatile boolean burn = true; // the code under test: settles on another thread, about 2 ms of work static Thread settleAsync(Runnable whenDone) { Thread t = new Thread(() -> { long end = System.nanoTime() + 2_000_000; while (System.nanoTime() < end) Thread.onSpinWait(); whenDone.run(); }); t.start(); return t; } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { for (int i = 0; i < 8; i++) { Thread b = new Thread(() -> { while (burn) Thread.onSpinWait(); }); // a busy machine b.setDaemon(true); b.start(); } int sleepFailed = 0, latchFailed = 0; for (int run = 0; run < 100; run++) { boolean[] settled = {false}; Thread t = settleAsync(() -> settled[0] = true); Thread.sleep(3); // "should be enough" if (!settled[0]) sleepFailed++; // (a racy read too, which is the point) t.join(); } for (int run = 0; run < 100; run++) { CountDownLatch settled = new CountDownLatch(1); settleAsync(settled::countDown); if (!settled.await(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) latchFailed++; // waits exactly as long as needed } burn = false; System.out.println("sleep(3) then assert: failed " + sleepFailed + " of 100"); System.out.println("latch.await(5 s): failed " + latchFailed + " of 100"); } }

alt.title: SleepVsLatch.kt
alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l13 import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit import kotlin.concurrent.thread // A test checks that a background worker settles a payment. One version sleeps 3 ms and hopes; // the other waits on a latch. Both run 100 times while 8 threads keep every core busy, like a CI box. @Volatile private var burn = true // the code under test: settles on another thread, about 2 ms of work private fun settleAsync(whenDone: () -> Unit): Thread = thread { val end = System.nanoTime() + 2_000_000 while (System.nanoTime() < end) Thread.onSpinWait() whenDone() } fun main() { repeat(8) { thread(isDaemon = true) { while (burn) Thread.onSpinWait() } } // a busy machine var sleepFailed = 0 var latchFailed = 0 repeat(100) { var settled = false val t = settleAsync { settled = true } Thread.sleep(3) // "should be enough" if (!settled) sleepFailed++ // (a racy read too, which is the point) t.join() } repeat(100) { val settled = CountDownLatch(1) settleAsync { settled.countDown() } if (!settled.await(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) latchFailed++ // waits exactly as long as needed } burn = false println("sleep(3) then assert: failed $sleepFailed of 100") println("latch.await(5 s): failed $latchFailed of 100") }

try.expect: The sleep version failed in about a quarter of the runs here (24 and 32 of 100). The latch version failed 0 times. A 10 ms sleep fails less often, but it can still fail, and it makes every run slower.

sections.h: Let jcstress search the interleavings for you
sections.html:
Some bugs need millions of attempts and a weak-memory CPU to show up at all. A weak-memory CPU, such as ARM, may let other cores see one core's writes in a different order than it made them. jcstress is the OpenJDK harness for exactly that. It runs tiny tests millions of times, with careful control over how threads start and where state lives, and counts every outcome it sees. The latest tagged release is 0.16, from February 2023; the master branch is 0.17-SNAPSHOT.

A test is a class with shared @State, two or more @Actor methods that run at the same time, and a result object, here II_Result with two int fields. @Outcome annotations say which results are allowed:

import org.openjdk.jcstress.annotations.*;
import org.openjdk.jcstress.infra.results.II_Result;
import static org.openjdk.jcstress.annotations.Expect.*;

@JCStressTest
@Outcome(id = "1, 2", expect = ACCEPTABLE, desc = "actor1 went first")
@Outcome(id = "2, 1", expect = ACCEPTABLE, desc = "actor2 went first")
@Outcome(id = "1, 1", expect = ACCEPTABLE_INTERESTING, desc = "both read 0: one increment lost")
@State
public class RefundCounterRace {
    int refunds;                                  // shared state, fresh for every sample

    @Actor
    public void actor1(II_Result r) { r.r1 = ++refunds; }

    @Actor
    public void actor2(II_Result r) { r.r2 = ++refunds; }
}

It is a Java-only tool: tests are processed by an annotation processor at build time, so there is no Kotlin twin here.

The outcome labels are the part to learn:

  • ACCEPTABLE is a correct result.
  • ACCEPTABLE_INTERESTING is allowed but worth seeing, usually the race the test is about. Here, "1, 1" means both actors read 0: an increment was lost.
  • FORBIDDEN must never happen. If jcstress observes it even once, the test fails.

For each test jcstress reports every observed outcome with how many times it occurred and its label. Results depend on the hardware: x86 keeps stores in order, so some memory-model anomalies that ARM machines (Apple Silicon, AWS Graviton) show regularly may never appear on an Intel laptop. Interesting means allowed, not guaranteed to appear.

The README documents a Maven archetype and no official Gradle setup, so try it in a separate Maven project. The jcstress samples on GitHub are a course in themselves; each has the outcomes it expects in its source.

try.title: Run a jcstress test (optional, needs Maven and network)
steps: In a scratch folder outside the labs, generate a jcstress project with the archetype command below (from the jcstress README).
Add RefundCounterRace from this section to the generated sources, build, and run only that test with -t.
Find the line for outcome 1, 1. Then change int refunds to an AtomicInteger and both actors to incrementAndGet(), rebuild and run again.

code.title: terminal
code.html: mvn archetype:generate -DinteractiveMode=false -DarchetypeGroupId=org.openjdk.jcstress \ -DarchetypeArtifactId=jcstress-java-test-archetype -DgroupId=org.sample -DartifactId=test -Dversion=1.0 cd test # put RefundCounterRace.java next to the generated sample test, then: mvn clean verify java -jar target/jcstress.jar -t RefundCounterRace

try.expect: The first run reports 1, 2 and 2, 1 as acceptable and 1, 1 as interesting, observed some percentage of the time (the jcstress samples record a few percent for this kind of test; your count will differ). With AtomicInteger, 1, 1 is never observed. If you mark 1, 1 as FORBIDDEN in the racy version, the test fails.

sections.h: When it hangs, take dumps; when it's slow, record JFR
sections.html:
In production you debug with what the JVM can tell you about itself. Two tools cover most cases.

A thread dump answers "where is every thread right now, and what is it waiting for". jcmd <pid> Thread.print -l prints each thread's state and stack, the java.util.concurrent locks it owns, and a deadlock report if there is a cycle (lesson 6 of this track). The state line is the first thing to read:

What the dump says What the thread is doing
RUNNABLE Running, ready to run, or blocked inside native I/O such as a socket read
BLOCKED (on object monitor) Waiting to enter a synchronized block that another thread holds
WAITING (parking) Parked by java.util.concurrent: a lock, latch, queue or semaphore; the parking to wait for line names it
WAITING (on object monitor) Inside Object.wait()
TIMED_WAITING The same, with a timeout, or in sleep

One dump is a photo. Take three, a few seconds apart. A thread in the same frame each time is stuck; a thread that moves is busy. Thirty threads WAITING (parking) on the same lock in every dump send you looking for its owner, which -l names. For tooling, Thread.dump_to_file -format=json writes JSON; on JDK 21 it has only names and stacks per thread, and from JDK 25 it adds state and lock fields.

Java Flight Recorder answers "what were threads waiting on over the last minute, and for how long". It is built into the JVM and cheap enough for production. jdk.JavaMonitorEnter records each wait to enter a synchronized block longer than a threshold, with the monitor's class, the duration and the previous owner. jdk.JavaMonitorWait covers Object.wait(), and jdk.ThreadPark covers ReentrantLock and the other java.util.concurrent waits. JDK 25 added jdk.JavaMonitorStatistics and jdk.JavaMonitorNotify.

jcmd <pid> Thread.print -l                          # states, stacks, owned j.u.c locks, deadlocks
jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json t.json  # JSON; per-thread state and lock fields need JDK 25+
jcmd <pid> JFR.start duration=60s filename=locks.jfr
jfr summary locks.jfr                               # how many events of each type
jfr print --events jdk.JavaMonitorEnter locks.jfr   # who waited for which monitor, how long, after whom

No JFR event reports deadlocks; for those, use a dump or ThreadMXBean. In a container the JVM is often PID 1, so jcmd 1 Thread.print inside the pod is the quickest start.

try.title: Record contention with JFR
steps: Read JfrContention. It starts a JFR recording from inside the program, runs six threads for one second (three fight over a monitor, three over a ReentrantLock), then reads the recording back.
Run it. Which event type does each kind of lock produce?
Run jfr summary and then jfr print --events jdk.JavaMonitorEnter on the file the demo printed. Find previousOwner.

code.title: JfrContention.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l13; import java.nio.file.Files; import java.nio.file.Path; import java.time.Duration; import java.util.Map; import java.util.TreeMap; import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock; import jdk.jfr.Recording; import jdk.jfr.consumer.RecordedEvent; import jdk.jfr.consumer.RecordingFile; /** * Records one second of lock contention with Java Flight Recorder, from inside the program, * then reads the recording back and summarizes it. The .jfr file is kept for the jfr tool. */ public class JfrContention { static final Object ledgerMonitor = new Object(); static final ReentrantLock batchLock = new ReentrantLock(); static void busy(long micros) { long end = System.nanoTime() + micros * 1_000; while (System.nanoTime() < end) Thread.onSpinWait(); } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { Path file = Files.createTempFile("contention-", ".jfr"); try (Recording rec = new Recording()) { rec.enable("jdk.JavaMonitorEnter").withThreshold(Duration.ofMillis(1)); // waited > 1 ms for a monitor rec.enable("jdk.ThreadPark").withThreshold(Duration.ofMillis(1)); // parked > 1 ms (j.u.c locks) rec.start(); long end = System.nanoTime() + 1_000_000_000L; Thread[] ts = new Thread[6]; for (int i = 0; i < ts.length; i++) { boolean useMonitor = i % 2 == 0; ts[i] = new Thread(() -> { while (System.nanoTime() < end) { if (useMonitor) { synchronized (ledgerMonitor) { busy(3_000); } // hold it 3 ms } else { batchLock.lock(); try { busy(3_000); } finally { batchLock.unlock(); } } } }, (useMonitor ? "ledger-" : "batch-") + i); ts[i].start(); } for (Thread t : ts) t.join(); rec.stop(); rec.dump(file); } Map<String, long[]> byKind = new TreeMap<>(); // count, total ms for (RecordedEvent e : RecordingFile.readAllEvents(file)) { String what = switch (e.getEventType().getName()) { case "jdk.JavaMonitorEnter" -> "JavaMonitorEnter on " + e.getClass("monitorClass").getName(); case "jdk.ThreadPark" -> "ThreadPark on " + (e.getClass("parkedClass") == null ? "?" : e.getClass("parkedClass").getName()); default -> e.getEventType().getName(); }; long[] agg = byKind.computeIfAbsent(what, k -> new long[2]); agg[0]++; agg[1] += e.getDuration().toMillis(); } byKind.forEach((k, v) -> System.out.printf("%-70s %5d events, %6d ms waiting%n", k, v[0], v[1])); System.out.println("recording kept at " + file); } }

alt.title: JfrContention.kt
alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l13 import java.nio.file.Files import java.time.Duration import java.util.TreeMap import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock import jdk.jfr.Recording import jdk.jfr.consumer.RecordingFile import kotlin.concurrent.thread import kotlin.concurrent.withLock // Records one second of lock contention with Java Flight Recorder, from inside the program, // then reads the recording back and summarizes it. The .jfr file is kept for the jfr tool. private val ledgerMonitor = Any() private val batchLock = ReentrantLock() private fun busy(micros: Long) { val end = System.nanoTime() + micros * 1_000 while (System.nanoTime() < end) Thread.onSpinWait() } fun main() { val file = Files.createTempFile("contention-", ".jfr") Recording().use { rec -> rec.enable("jdk.JavaMonitorEnter").withThreshold(Duration.ofMillis(1)) // waited > 1 ms for a monitor rec.enable("jdk.ThreadPark").withThreshold(Duration.ofMillis(1)) // parked > 1 ms (j.u.c locks) rec.start() val end = System.nanoTime() + 1_000_000_000L val ts = List(6) { i -> val useMonitor = i % 2 == 0 thread(name = (if (useMonitor) "ledger-" else "batch-") + i) { while (System.nanoTime() < end) { if (useMonitor) synchronized(ledgerMonitor) { busy(3_000) } // hold it 3 ms else batchLock.withLock { busy(3_000) } } } } ts.forEach { it.join() } rec.stop() rec.dump(file) } val byKind = TreeMap<String, LongArray>() // count, total ms for (e in RecordingFile.readAllEvents(file)) { val what = when (e.eventType.name) { "jdk.JavaMonitorEnter" -> "JavaMonitorEnter on " + e.getClass("monitorClass").name "jdk.ThreadPark" -> "ThreadPark on " + (e.getClass("parkedClass")?.name ?: "?") else -> e.eventType.name } val agg = byKind.getOrPut(what) { LongArray(2) } agg[0]++ agg[1] += e.duration.toMillis() } byKind.forEach { (k, v) -> println("%-70s %5d events, %6d ms waiting".format(k, v[0], v[1])) } println("recording kept at $file") }

try.expect: Two lines: JavaMonitorEnter on java.lang.Object for the synchronized threads and ThreadPark on java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock$NonfairSync for the explicit lock, each with a hundred or more events and about a second of total waiting. jfr print shows each event's duration, monitorClass, previousOwner (the thread that held the monitor) and the waiting thread's stack.

analogy: A stress test is a crash test: you don't learn anything by driving the car gently around the car park; you build a fresh car, drive it into the wall at speed, inspect it, and do it again many times. Replacing sleeps with latches is the difference between "wait ten minutes, then check whether the pizza arrived" and "open the door when the bell rings". jcstress is a test track that drives millions of cars in slightly different ways and records every kind of damage. A thread dump is a photo of the traffic; JFR is the traffic camera's recording. The analogy breaks at the crash test: a car that survived a thousand crashes really is strong. Code that passed a thousand stress rounds may still have a race the test never hit.
world: In a Quarkus service, keep stress tests in their own JUnit tag so the normal build stays fast, and run them on CI where machines are busy, since busy machines interleave more. Integration tests with Testcontainers, Kafka and Oracle check wiring, not thread safety; they run too few concurrent operations to find a race. When a pod stops answering, take three thread dumps before anyone restarts it: kubectl exec <pod> -- jcmd 1 Thread.print -l works when the JVM is PID 1. When latency creeps up without errors, start a JFR recording on the pod and look at JavaMonitorEnter and ThreadPark: a lock that every request waits on shows up as hundreds of events on the same class.
mistake: The most common mistake is fixing a flaky concurrency test by tuning it until it passes: a longer sleep, a retry annotation, a CI rule that reruns failures. Flakiness in a concurrency test is often the only symptom a real race ever shows before production. Every retry hides it a little better. The fix is to find out why the test is flaky. If the test guesses at timing, replace the sleep with a latch or a deadline-bounded wait. If the code is racy, the test just did its job, so fix the code and keep the test.

compare.title: The same stress test in Java and Kotlin

java.title: Java (JUnit 6)
java.html: @RepeatedTest(5) // a race test is a sample: take several @Timeout(10) // a deadlock fails the test instead of hanging the build void noRefundIsLost() throws Exception { RefundLedger ledger = new RefundLedger(Map.of("pay-1", 10_000L)); AtomicLong approved = new AtomicLong(); CountDownLatch go = new CountDownLatch(1); List<Thread> threads = new ArrayList<>(); for (int t = 0; t < 8; t++) { // more threads than cores Thread th = new Thread(() -> { try { go.await(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; } for (int i = 0; i < 2_000; i++) if (ledger.refund("pay-1", 1)) approved.incrementAndGet(); }); th.start(); threads.add(th); } go.countDown(); // the starting gun for (Thread th : threads) th.join(); assertThat(approved.get()).isEqualTo(10_000); // an invariant, not a timing assertThat(ledger.refunded("pay-1")).isEqualTo(10_000); }

kotlin.title: Kotlin (JUnit 6)
kotlin.html: @RepeatedTest(5) // a race test is a sample: take several @Timeout(10) // a deadlock fails the test instead of hanging the build fun `no refund is lost`() { val ledger = RefundLedger(mapOf("pay-1" to 10_000L)) val approved = AtomicLong() val go = CountDownLatch(1) val threads = List(8) { // more threads than cores thread { go.await() repeat(2_000) { if (ledger.refund("pay-1", 1)) approved.incrementAndGet() } } } go.countDown() // the starting gun threads.forEach { it.join() } assertThat(approved.get()).isEqualTo(10_000L) // an invariant, not a timing assertThat(ledger.refunded("pay-1")).isEqualTo(10_000L) }

compare.note: JUnit, AssertJ and the latches work the same from both languages. Kotlin removes ceremony: thread { } starts a thread in one line, List(8) { ... } collects them, and with no checked exceptions there is no try/catch around go.await(). Two details differ. Backtick test names read like specs. And AssertJ needs 10_000L in Kotlin: assertThat(aLong).isEqualTo(10_000) would pass an Int, which picks the Object overload and fails because Long 10,000 isn't equal to Integer 10,000. For coroutine code, Kotlin has a tool Java lacks: kotlinx-coroutines-test runs suspending code on virtual time, so tests of delays and timeouts run instantly and deterministically. The coroutines track covers it.

worked.title: Turn a flaky "loads once" test into a deterministic one

steps.say: This test is meant to prove that BinCache from lesson 9 loads a BIN once when eight callers ask together. Read it and decide what it actually tests.
steps.code: @Test void loadsOnce() throws Exception { AtomicInteger loads = new AtomicInteger(); BinCache cache = new BinCache(bin -> { loads.incrementAndGet(); return "Northwind Bank"; }); for (int i = 0; i < 8; i++) new Thread(() -> cache.issuerFor("411111")).start(); Thread.sleep(100); // "they should be done by now" assertThat(loads.get()).isEqualTo(1); }

alt.html: @Test fun `loads once`() { val loads = AtomicInteger() val cache = BinCache { loads.incrementAndGet(); "Northwind Bank" } repeat(8) { thread { cache.issuerFor("411111") } } Thread.sleep(100) // "they should be done by now" assertThat(loads.get()).isEqualTo(1) }

steps.say: It tests the scheduler. The loader is so fast that the threads rarely overlap, so the racy get-then-put cache passes too. And on a slow machine the threads might not have run at all within 100 ms, so loads is 0 and a correct cache fails. The fix is to control the timing: hold the first load inside the loader until every caller is known to be waiting, then let it go.
Here is the deterministic version, with subgoal labels. The loader blocks on a latch, and the test polls thread states, with a deadline, until all eight callers are parked.
steps.code: @Test @Timeout(10) void loadsOnceWhileOthersWait() throws Exception { AtomicInteger loads = new AtomicInteger(); CountDownLatch inLoader = new CountDownLatch(1), release = new CountDownLatch(1); BinCache cache = new BinCache(bin -> { loads.incrementAndGet(); inLoader.countDown(); // 1. a caller is inside the loader try { release.await(); } // and stays there until we say go catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } return "Northwind Bank"; }); List<Thread> callers = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < 8; i++) { Thread t = new Thread(() -> cache.issuerFor("411111")); t.start(); callers.add(t); } assertThat(inLoader.await(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS)).isTrue(); awaitParked(callers, 8); // 2. all 8 are now waiting, inside or outside release.countDown(); // 3. let the load finish for (Thread t : callers) t.join(); assertThat(loads.get()).isEqualTo(1); // 4. one load served all eight } static void awaitParked(List<Thread> threads, int n) throws InterruptedException { long deadline = System.nanoTime() + TimeUnit.SECONDS.toNanos(5); while (threads.stream().filter(t -> t.getState() == Thread.State.BLOCKED || t.getState() == Thread.State.WAITING).count() < n) { if (System.nanoTime() > deadline) throw new AssertionError("callers never queued up"); Thread.sleep(5); // polling with a deadline: never a bare guess } }

alt.html: @Test @Timeout(10) fun `loads once while others wait`() { val loads = AtomicInteger() val inLoader = CountDownLatch(1) val release = CountDownLatch(1) val cache = BinCache { loads.incrementAndGet() inLoader.countDown() // 1. a caller is inside the loader release.await() // and stays there until we say go "Northwind Bank" } val callers = List(8) { thread { cache.issuerFor("411111") } } assertThat(inLoader.await(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS)).isTrue() awaitParked(callers, 8) // 2. all 8 are now waiting, inside or outside release.countDown() // 3. let the load finish callers.forEach { it.join() } assertThat(loads.get()).isEqualTo(1) // 4. one load served all eight } fun awaitParked(threads: List<Thread>, n: Int) { val deadline = System.nanoTime() + TimeUnit.SECONDS.toNanos(5) while (threads.count { it.state == Thread.State.BLOCKED || it.state == Thread.State.WAITING } < n) { check(System.nanoTime() < deadline) { "callers never queued up" } Thread.sleep(5) // polling with a deadline: never a bare guess } }

steps.say: Before reading on, explain to yourself why this version fails on the racy cache every time. Answer: with get-then-put, every caller misses and enters the loader, so all eight end up waiting on release inside it, and step 2 is satisfied. When the test opens the latch, all eight loads finish and loads is 8. With computeIfAbsent, one caller is inside the loader and the other seven are BLOCKED on the map's bin, so loads is 1. The outcome no longer depends on luck, only on the code.

lab.title: A stress harness that catches races, and a refund race to fix
steps: Run the tests. Six of seven fail. The five Stress tests hit UnsupportedOperationException. The ledger load test approves 16,000 one-cent refunds against 10,000 captured.

Write Stress.failingRounds. For each round: call setup, create ready and go latches, start threads threads that count down ready, wait on go, then run the actor perThread times. Wait on ready, count down go, join every thread, then test the invariant and count the failures.
Run the tests again. The Stress tests should pass, including the two that point your harness at racy code (a volatile counter and a check-then-act ledger) and expect it to find failures.
Fix RefundLedger.refund: do the check and the update inside one refunded.compute(...) call, and call writeAuditLine() after it, only when the refund was approved.
Run the tests until all seven pass, then twice more.
hints: The start line is the Hammer from lesson 3 of this track. Make the actor threads daemons, so a stuck actor can't keep the JVM alive.
The join() does two jobs: it waits, and it makes everything the actors wrote visible to the thread that checks the invariant.
Inside compute, return already unchanged (it may be null) to reject a refund. Record the decision in a local boolean[1] or an AtomicBoolean, because a lambda can't assign a local variable.
lab.done: All seven tests in ConcurrencyTestingTest pass, three runs in a row.

drill.title: A stress test from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write a JUnit test that checks a Counter (with increment() and total()) loses nothing when 8 threads each call increment() 50,000 times. Check: do the threads start together, does a deadlock fail the test, and is your assertion an invariant rather than a timing?

answer.html: @Test @Timeout(10) void countsEveryIncrement() throws Exception { Counter counter = new Counter(); CountDownLatch go = new CountDownLatch(1); List<Thread> threads = new ArrayList<>(); for (int t = 0; t < 8; t++) { Thread th = new Thread(() -> { try { go.await(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; } for (int i = 0; i < 50_000; i++) counter.increment(); }); th.start(); threads.add(th); } go.countDown(); for (Thread th : threads) th.join(); assertThat(counter.total()).isEqualTo(8 * 50_000); }

alt.title: Kotlin
alt.html: @Test @Timeout(10) fun `counts every increment from 8 threads`() { val counter = Counter() val go = CountDownLatch(1) val threads = List(8) { thread { go.await(); repeat(50_000) { counter.increment() } } } go.countDown() threads.forEach { it.join() } assertThat(counter.total()).isEqualTo(8 * 50_000) }

recap: A stress test forces overlap: a start latch, more threads than cores, many operations, many rounds with fresh state, and an invariant checked after join().
Every concurrency test gets a timeout. A pass means "not found this time", never "proven correct".
Replace Thread.sleep with latches, futures or deadline-bounded polling. A fake that blocks on a latch holds a thread at a known point.
jcstress runs tiny tests millions of times and labels outcomes ACCEPTABLE, ACCEPTABLE_INTERESTING or FORBIDDEN; any forbidden outcome fails the test.
Thread dumps show where threads are and what they wait for; take several, seconds apart. JFR's JavaMonitorEnter and ThreadPark show contention over time.

explain.prompt: A teammate says: "Our concurrency test has been green for months, so the class is thread-safe." Explain what a green stress test does and doesn't tell you, and what you'd check about the test itself.
explain.answer: A green run means the test didn't happen to hit a bad interleaving, not that none exists. Races depend on timing, hardware and load, so a test can stay green for months and the race still fire in production. I'd check that the test actually makes threads collide: a start latch, more threads than cores, enough operations per thread, many rounds with fresh state, and an assertion on an invariant rather than timing. I'd check that it has a timeout so a deadlock would fail it. And I'd still review the class against the rules: what state is shared, which lock or atomic protects each compound action, and whether anything calls out while holding a lock. Tests find races; design prevents them.

deeper.html:
jcstress has more than actors and outcomes. An @Arbiter method runs after all actors have finished and can record the final state into the result, which suits tests like "after two increments, is the counter 2?". Termination tests, marked @JCStressTest(Mode.Termination) with a @Signal method, check whether a thread ever notices a signal; the sample BasicJMM_04_Progress uses this to show whether a spin loop ever sees a field change. The runner has modes too: the README mentions -m quick, which many CI setups use to keep runs short.

For Kotlin code, JetBrains' Lincheck library tests concurrent data structures by running operations from several threads, including in a model-checking mode that explores interleavings systematically, and then checking that the results match some sequential order of the same operations. It is worth a look before you write a lock-free structure.

JFR is not only a file format. jdk.jfr.consumer.RecordingStream, added in JDK 14 (JEP 349), streams events to your code while the program runs. A service can subscribe to jdk.JavaMonitorEnter and export a metric when waits on one class exceed a budget.

Finally, the JDK's own tools can be scripted. jcmd <pid> help lists every diagnostic command a JVM supports, and the list changes between versions: JDK 24 added Thread.vthread_scheduler and Thread.vthread_pollers for virtual threads, and from JDK 24 Thread.print also includes virtual threads that are mounted on a carrier. The virtual threads track uses those.
